Qnergy builds Stirling engines for remote power, putting a two-century-old engine design to work in commercial equipment. Its sealed QB80 engine turns heat from an external source into power, keeping fuel contaminants away from its moving parts. That design helps meet the demand for dependable electricity at remote oil sites, according to Two Bit da Vinci.

Explore how the Stirling cycle moves gas between hot and cold ends, and how a regenerator recovers heat between strokes. You can also see why sealed components and precise manufacturing matter, along with the limits imposed by cost and fuel efficiency. Then compare the engine’s uses in compressed-air equipment and landfill methane destruction.

Qnergy builds Stirling engines for remote power, compressed air and landfill methane destruction. It has about 5,000 units operating in the field and was profitable as of 2024. The QB80 powers the 5.65 kW PowerGen 5650 generator. Its sealed engine has no oil, internal filters or scheduled service interval, and is rated for 70,000 to 80,000 operating hours. Qnergy’s compressed-air equipment replaces gas-powered pneumatic functions at oil wells, reducing methane venting. Alliance Technical Group measured 99.998% methane destruction for the Qnergy package using EPA test methods. At a closed landfill in Weber County, a Stirling engine powers a blower and combustor using landfill gas. A project representative says the system can extract and destroy the gas autonomously; Qnergy’s carbon credits filing says credit revenue is the only funding source for its landfill projects. The complete Qnergy package converts around 12% of its fuel into electricity and carries premium pricing. Its sealed engine is basically maintenance-free for a decade, but the overall system still needs technician attention.

Qnergy builds and ships Stirling engines for remote power, compressed air and landfill methane destruction. The company has about 5,000 units operating in the field and was profitable as of 2024.

Qnergy has found commercial uses for an engine that remained outside the mass market for two centuries because of its cost and a lack of suitable applications. Its QB80 engine uses heat from outside a sealed cylinder to generate power, keeping fuel contaminants away from the moving parts.

The QB80 powers Qnergy’s PowerGen 5650 generator package. The engine is a welded steel cylinder roughly the size of a scuba tank. It has no oil, internal filters or scheduled service interval, and is welded shut in Ogden.

Remote oil sites are one market for the generator, and customers include major oil-industry players. A power failure can cost a site up to $50,000 a day and require technicians to reach it by helicopter. At such sites, PowerGen holds up where equipment such as diesel generators could not. Customers pay for uptime rather than fuel efficiency or emissions benefits.

Qnergy also sells compressed air pneumatics, or CAP, equipment. Oil-well operators can use natural gas from the ground to power tools and then vent it. Qnergy’s equipment replaces that gas-powered function with compressed air. Avoiding the venting also reduces methane emissions: methane traps about 80 times as much heat as carbon dioxide over a 20-year period.

A Qnergy representative says a gas connection can produce compressed air and electricity within 20 minutes, while waste heat can prevent freezing in cold environments. The higher-airflow CAP V can run from a PowerGen or the grid. The representative says the kits have become a major revenue source in the last few years.

Qnergy’s white paper relied on an EPA rule requiring US oil and gas operators to replace venting pneumatic controllers. Congress repealed the waste-emission charge in February 2025 and blocked its collection until 2034. The EPA loosened flare and vent gas requirements in April 2026.

Alliance Technical Group measured 99.998% methane destruction for the Qnergy package using EPA test methods. It measured carbon monoxide at 27 times below EPA limits and nitrogen oxides at seven times below them. A separate evaluator funded by the Canadian government found that the Qnergy generator had the highest carbon-chain destruction efficiency among the generation technologies assessed.

Deep dive into the latest in energy by exploring our other resources and articles.

Landfills continue producing methane for decades after they close. Electricity plants can burn the gas when output is high, but generation stops making economic sense once production falls below a threshold. The US has more than 10,000 closed landfills.

Landfill gas contains hydrogen sulfide and siloxanes from discarded cosmetics and detergents. Burning siloxanes creates silicon dioxide. In a conventional generator, deposits could bog down the engine and require an overhaul every six months to a year. A Stirling engine keeps the fuel outside its sealed working parts, so it can use heat from burning the gas without sending it through the engine.

At Torch 4, a trailer near a closed landfill in Weber County, a Stirling engine powers a blower and combustor using gas drawn from the ground. The system also includes instrumentation. A project representative says it can extract and destroy landfill gas autonomously, without grid or external power.

Qnergy’s carbon credits filing says credit revenue is the only funding source for its landfill projects. The projects aim to destroy methane and earn credits rather than make electricity generation profitable.

Robert Stirling patented the engine on September 27, 1816, eight days after his Church of Scotland ordination. Steam-boiler explosions had killed people, including members of his parish. His design kept the fire outside the machine and removed the boiler that could burst.

A displacer moves sealed working gas between hot and cold ends, cycling it between hundreds and tens of degrees Celsius 60 times per second. The gas expands and raises pressure at the hot end, then contracts as it cools. A second piston responds to the pressure changes and extracts power. Fuel contaminants do not contact the moving parts, avoiding the combustion residue that can contribute to early wear in internal-combustion engines.

Between the heat exchangers, a fine-mesh regenerator, which Stirling called the “economizer,” stores heat from gas travelling toward the cold end and returns it as the gas moves back. The engine can turn without it, but sending hot gas straight to the cold exchanger would waste most of the heat on each stroke. Its design must balance heat-storage surface area against flow resistance, because pressure lost to pumping reduces generating power. Qnergy’s engineers still devote substantial attention to it.

Qnergy’s free-piston design has no crankshaft. The piston and displacer move on springs at a resonant frequency near 60 hertz, without a mechanical stop or linkage limiting travel.

Power electronics control piston amplitude and temperature, using the generating alternator as a brake: drawing more current shortens the stroke, while drawing less increases it. Without restraint every millisecond, the piston could travel out of control and damage the engine. Sufficiently fast, affordable electronics for continuous control did not arrive until the 1990s.

That fixed-frequency operation also limits use in cars. In a car engine, fuel burns inside the cylinder and pushes a piston connected to a crankshaft; the stroke is fixed and cycle speed changes power. A Stirling-powered Ford Torino built by Philips and Ford in 1975 returned 10% to 20% worse fuel economy than the petrol car it was intended to replace. The free-piston design is also considered unsuitable for airplanes.

Inside the QB80, a clearance seal leaves a gap of a few microns between the piston and its bore. It prevents gas from passing without contact or friction; the engine has no piston rings. Spiral flexure bearings keep the displacer aligned while allowing it to move along its operating axis. They provide the spring rate and resonant frequency while resisting radial movement that could cause rubbing. Oil is unsuitable inside the engine because it would clog the regenerator’s mesh.

The working gas is helium, which is difficult to contain. About 400 laser welds must hold it inside the assembly. Laser welding concentrates heat in a small area, whereas the heat from TIG welding could distort parts with micron-scale clearances. Manufacturing decisions and quality assurance are critical because the engine is not reopened after welding. Hydrogen would be better thermodynamically, but it embrittles metals and is dangerous to work with.

Qnergy machines its own engine components because it cannot buy Stirling-engine parts from an established supply chain at scale. Stirling engines also have low power density and high build costs. As an engine grows, the surface that admits heat increases with the square of its radius, while the gas volume grows with the cube. That makes larger designs harder to heat.

Stirling engines have historically competed with diesel and natural-gas generators but have not been expected to beat them on cost and efficiency. Nearly silent Stirling engines power air-independent propulsion in Gotland-class submarines, which can remain submerged for weeks. In 2005 war games, a Swedish submarine virtually torpedoed the USS Ronald Reagan undetected.

The complete Qnergy package converts only around 12% of its fuel into electricity, and its pricing is deliberately premium. The sealed engine is basically maintenance-free for a decade, but the overall system still needs a technician to clean the radiator and check airflow and filters. Qnergy is working on engines intended to cost half as much and hazardous-location units for offshore rigs; its work on solar dishes and small modular reactors is non-commercial and will take time.

For operators seeking reliable power at remote oil sites, Qnergy’s PowerGen 5650 is worth checking out in more detail as an alternative to generators that struggle in those conditions.

Swift is a single-cell lithium-ion FPV quadcopter built for longer flights, with a carbon frame that accommodates a choice of electronics and battery sizes. Its interchangeable trays fit either an 18650 or a larger 21700 cell. Swift flew more than 5 km, though its video signal weakened near that distance in windy conditions, according to Mediocre Nerd.

Compare 18650 and 21700 cells for their effects on flight time and handling, and see how the frame accommodates analog or digital electronics. You can also review the battery-holder test, including how the DIY holder retained voltage under load, along with the signal warnings and headwinds that complicated the long-distance return flight.

Swift is a single-cell lithium-ion FPV quad with a dead-cat frame that keeps the front arms out of the camera’s view. Builders can choose their own electronics and an analog or digital system. The initial build flew for 20 minutes. With 21700 cells, it flew for 27 minutes on an RS50 and reached 34 minutes on a Link Data 65P before telemetry was lost. In a full-throttle power-delivery test, the DIY battery holder had the lowest calculated resistance and best overall voltage retention. Mediocre Nerd considers all four tested connections viable given the close results. After the original carbon-fiber frame cracked, Swift was rebuilt with a thicker frame and larger 11,500 kV motors. The new motors provided better acceleration and handling, more low-end torque, and lower current draw. On a lake flight approaching 5 km, video-signal warnings and strong wind constrained the return. Mediocre Nerd warns that GPS return to home might not work reliably in a fail-safe under those windy conditions.

Lithium-ion cells have much higher energy density than lithium polymer batteries. An example 18650 cell has a 3,000 mA capacity and weighs just under 45 g. Three LiPos with a combined capacity of 2,000 mA weigh 48 g. In that comparison, the 18650 supplies 50% more capacity at roughly the same weight.

Long flight times do not remove every range constraint. Your video transmitter may lack power, your receiver may have an unsuitable antenna, or your flight controller may not support GPS. Swift’s build addresses those components alongside the battery and frame.

Larger 21700 cells have greater energy density than 18650s, but they also add size and weight. They are expected to trade some flight performance for longer endurance. In testing, the 18650 handled better, although the 21700’s flight performance exceeded expectations.

Swift’s dead cat layout extends the front arms straight out to the sides, keeping them out of the camera’s view. The frame also has reinforced arms and mounting options intended to accommodate most electronics. You can choose your own electronics and use either an analog or digital system.

The earlier Crux 3 frame is extremely light but lacks durability and mounting options. The Lion B is heavier and stiffer than the Crux, with more room for electronics, but it fits only its proprietary electronics and seems somewhat brittle. Swift’s frame is slightly thinner and lighter than the Lion B, with more flex that can help absorb impacts in some cases.

A 3 mm Swift cutout weighed about 15 g and was relatively stiff, which can help with tuning and performance. The initial build used a lighter 9 g version instead. A later rebuild used a thicker 2.5 mm frame after the earlier carbon-fiber frame cracked. The build used these components and dimensions:

An ND filter and adapter protect the camera lens in a crash and were chosen in the hope of reducing image distortion. Mediocre Nerd rates the DJI O4 Lite best in class for video quality and transmission distance.

The canopy bolts to the frame from below. The battery tray sits on the front standoffs and is secured at its corners. Rear TPU mounts fit most receiver T-type antennas. Plastic nylon bolts were planned for the flight controller and video transmitter to save weight, with metal M2 bolts for the standoffs, motors and camera.

The two battery holders use 0.2 mm copper strip, 10 mm wide, and 18-gauge wire. You can cut the strip with ordinary scissors, leave a small overhang and fold it flat into the holder. The wire and copper ends are tinned with solder, with flux applied to the copper. The finished wires can take a plug or be soldered directly to the power leads.

The terminals need clear positive and negative markings: connecting a cell backwards once can destroy the electronics. In the build, the soldering iron was kept around 370 degrees Celsius, and the thin copper strips soldered fairly easily.

For the power-delivery test, the quad was secured and run at 100% throttle for 10 seconds per trial. Wire gauge and length were kept as similar as possible while the BT2.0, XT30, Lion battery holder and DIY holder were compared using voltage and current data recorded through the goggles.

The DIY holder had the lowest calculated resistance and the best voltage retention overall. It also had the smallest initial voltage sag, although it later fell behind the XT30 plug. Mediocre Nerd considers all four viable given the close results and guesses that copper conductivity and the DIY holder’s large contacts contributed to its result.

The data was logged to Lithium Ion FPV, which contains test descriptions, raw data, quadcopter builds and guides. It also ranks promising cells from Nelvik’s testing. Performance represents weight-to-power ratio, endurance represents capacity-to-weight ratio, and the two scores are averaged for an overall rating.

The initial Swift build was about 25 g heavier than the old Crux build, yet hovered at 30% throttle rather than 45%. The difference was attributed to the 15,000 kV motors. Swift handled well without tuning and felt similar to the Crux on a full-throttle takeoff, despite its heavier digital setup.

The initial build reached 20 minutes with 2.45 V remaining. The lighter Crux build, which had more efficient motors, had flown for 25 minutes.

The 66 g RS50 cell appeared to give Swift a maximum speed of around 80 km/h. Vibrations were visible and might mostly be tuned out. The board, which contains the ESCs, heated quickly under excessive throttle but cooled during cruising.

A long-distance flight with the 5,000 mA RS50 Reliance 21700 lasted 27 minutes, although there was no DVR footage because the goggles had no SD card. The Link Data 65P is about 5 g heavier, has a slightly lower discharge rating and a much higher capacity. It reached 30 minutes, was still flying at 2.39 V and reached 34 minutes before telemetry was lost.

Afterward, an exposed negative lead contacted metal at the back of the camera and shorted the air unit. Liquid electrical tape was applied to exposed metal and the canopy was modified to prevent another short. The tape dries in about five minutes to a rubbery layer.

The rebuild also replaced the motors with larger 1303 11,500 kV units. They added 4 g, while the motors and thicker frame together added about 7 g. In that configuration, the motors gave more low-end torque, better acceleration and handling, and lower current draw. More efficient propeller operation is a possible explanation.

With tuning, Swift produced smooth footage on its lake flight. Its display showed current, speed, throttle, battery voltage, distance, flight-controller temperature, radio and video signal health, flight time and GPS satellite count. GPS return to home requires at least eight satellites, while more satellites improve location accuracy.

The video signal produced yellow and red warnings as Swift approached 5 km in wind. It dipped during the turn toward home and stabilized after the drone reoriented. Mediocre Nerd warns that GPS return to home might not work reliably in a fail-safe under those windy conditions.

An estimated 35 km/h tailwind helped Swift reach 90 km/h at 50% throttle on the outbound leg. On the return, an estimated 40 km/h headwind gust slowed it, and current draw doubled from the outbound 10-12 amps to travel above 30 km/h. Descending appeared to help speed, although the quad still drew more than 20 amps. Swift reached shore with the battery at 3 V.

The earlier frame cracked, while professionally manufactured frames felt stronger and did not crack under pressur”e; carbon quality was considered the main issue. The planned Swift kit contains the custom frame, hardware and both battery trays, but builders must supply their chosen electronics and battery.

The results show that the configuration reached its distance and flight-time goals, while the signal warnings and wind on the lake flight show the conditions that constrained its return.

Claude Code lets you delegate coding and other work to Claude, with controls for commands, instructions and review. Instead of watching every step, you can assign tasks across separate sessions and inspect the results. Anthropic engineer Lydia Hallie explains how her team manages that work in a discussion presented by Nate Herk.

Explore how Claude Code uses CLAUDE.md instructions to supply context without crowding out the task. This deep dive also covers command approvals and deny rules for protecting sensitive files, along with checks and hooks that help verify results. You can use those distinctions to decide which instructions to keep and which safeguards to configure.

Keep CLAUDE.md focused on information Claude cannot infer from the code. Hi says emphatic rules can work against strong models; /doctor prompt audit can identify unnecessary or confusing instructions. Auto mode checks commands and asks for approval when unsure. In an August study, it blocked 89% of dangerous commands, while about 14% of people caught a clearly dangerous command; about one in 10 dangerous commands still passed auto mode. Deny rules can block access to sensitive files, but they inspect commands rather than everything those commands do. A sandbox limits file and website access; cloud sessions run on fresh computers without your keys, though pushed commits and connector messages persist. Checks, goal prompts and hooks help verify results during and after tasks. Hi says exit code 2 sends Claude back to fix a failed test, while Claude Code marks the task complete with exit code 1. Claude Code projects can delegate task-list items to separate sessions coordinated by a main session. Projects is in beta on Pro, Max and Ultra plans.

Claude Code can read a project’s CLAUDE.md file for instructions and context. Earlier workflows often involved watching a session, correcting it and adding emphatic rules to the file. Hi says those emphatic lines can work against you with models as strong as Claude Opus 5.5. Unnecessary instructions can send the model off track, increase tool calls and worsen results.

The file is best reserved for information Claude cannot infer from the code. It can serve as a routing map to a business wiki, brand assets and financial files. Claude Code can also use AGENTS.md for that purpose. You can audit CLAUDE.md and skills against the model you use with:

The audit can identify instructions the model no longer needs or material that takes up space. It may also find content that confuses the model.

Auto mode is the default in the terminal and Claude Code desktop app. A separate classifier checks commands. It allows actions such as tests and installs, but stops for approval when it is unsure. By default, it trusts only the current folder and repository, so a push to a separate deployment repository returns to you for approval.

Settings written in plain English tell the classifier which repositories, buckets and domains to trust, as well as what to always allow or never do. Claude Code can draft settings entries from a project and recent sessions with:

In an August study comparing auto mode with people in the loop, about 14% of people caught a clearly dangerous command, while auto mode blocked 89% of the dangerous commands. About one in 10 still passed through auto mode.

A deny rule adds a hard block in the settings file that Claude Code can check before auto mode. Hi’s criterion for a deny-list entry is whether you can undo a mistake. You can reverse bad code, but you cannot undo the reading of an API key or the wiping of unsaved work. A permission rule can block access to the .env file rather than relying on an instruction in a prompt.

That distinction matters for client work and knowledge work, too. You can rewrite a draft, but you cannot take back a sent email or a deleted file. A deny rule sees the command rather than everything it does. A compromised test script could still try to read an .env file or SSH keys and send them to an unfamiliar server.

A sandbox limits which files a command can open and which websites it can reach. To configure it, enter:

For longer jobs, a cloud session runs on a fresh computer with a copy of your code but without your keys. It continues after you close your laptop. Deny rules committed to the project carry into future cloud sessions. The cloud machine is disposable, but a pushed commit or a message sent through a connector is not.

Learn more about Claude Code features and practices with other articles and guides we have written below.

Checks let Claude assess its output during a long task. The same request to move a login system to a new API could leave the old API in place, move only new logins or log everyone out. A check can catch a bad result before the run finishes.

Checks can be programmatic or describe what a good result should look like. For a research report, they could check that claims have source links or that numbers match a spreadsheet. Claude can also take screenshots and inspect its output. Hi prefers asking to see the actual output because she was not present while it was produced.

A goal prompt asks Claude to keep working until a defined finish line is true:

For checks that must run every time, hooks are scripts Claude Code runs automatically. They can check formatting after each edit, run a test after each task or run the full test suite before completion. Hi says most tools return exit code 1 when a test fails, but Claude Code marks the task complete with that code. Exit code 2 sends Claude back to fix the failure.

Once a session opens a pull request, continuous integration can run. On Hi’s team, a separate Claude session reviews every pull request first, and another group of agents double-checks each bug it finds. People review risky changes, while small changes such as documentation can merge after checks pass.

A Claude Code projects session can take a task list, start a separate session for each item and check the results. The list can cover code or work such as a client report, research brief, content ideas or scripts, while you talk to one main chat.

The main session coordinates rather than writing the code itself. Project settings let you choose a coordinator model and a thread model: Fable 52 could coordinate, while Opus 5.5 could carry out work in the individual threads. Hi identifies Fable as suited to deciding what to do and judging returned work.

Claude Code projects is in beta on Pro, Max and Ultra plans. Auto mode settings and deny rules govern different parts of command approval, and a deny rule alone does not inspect everything a command runs. Cloud sessions also need project-committed deny rules to carry those blocks into future sessions.

If you want to delegate coding or knowledge work and check the results, take a closer look at Claude Code for managing tasks across sessions.

Copilot in Excel helps you analyze spreadsheet data and work with formulas, tables and charts through natural-language requests. It can now work with locally saved workbooks, rather than requiring every file to be stored in OneDrive or SharePoint. Its chat, planning and editing modes offer different levels of control over changes, according to My Online Training Hub.

Explore how saved preferences and workbook rules give Copilot instructions across files or within a specific workbook. The deep dive also explains how to create a reusable skill for a monthly sales summary, including a table and chart. Finally, see how to connect permitted Power BI data and check Copilot’s calculations before relying on the results.

Copilot offers Chat only, Plan and allow editing modes. The review recommends Plan for requests that could make substantial changes, so you can review the approach before allowing edits. Personalization saves account-wide preferences, while workbook rules provide file-specific guidance in a visible .rules sheet. Shared workbooks retain their rules, but not personal preferences. Skills let you reuse instructions across workbooks, including built-in options for branding, design and finance. Python skill availability is still rolling out, so options can differ between users. Custom skills use written instructions in a skill.md file stored in a matching OneDrive subfolder. They are available in Excel for Windows, Mac and the web, though access can depend on licensing, update channel and organizational settings. Copilot can draw on web, Microsoft 365 work account, Power BI and external connector data, subject to access and configuration. My Online Training Hub recommends checking Copilot’s calculations rather than assuming a polished report is accurate.

You can open Copilot through the dynamic action button at the bottom right of Excel. Right-click the button to dock it on the right or move it back to the ribbon.

Above the chat prompt, three modes control what Copilot can do. Chat only answers questions and analyzes the workbook without changing it. Plan proposes steps for you to review, while allow editing permits changes such as editing cells, adding formulas and creating sheets.

The review recommends Plan for requests that could make substantial changes, so you can review the proposed approach before allowing edits. The models in the menu depend on your subscription and, for work accounts, the options your administrator has allowed. A manual model choice lasts for the current session; Excel returns to its default afterward.

Personalization saves preferences to your account and applies them across workbooks. Open Personalization from the three-dot menu, then add short, specific instructions on separate lines. For example, you can specify that Copilot should not merge cells or use currency formats in table columns.

These preferences do not travel with a workbook when you share it. A prompt that asks for something different also overrides a saved preference.

Workbook rules, by contrast, belong to one file. They can define its terminology, conventions and calculation methods, or identify sheets Copilot should not change. Copilot uses the rules as guidance in that file, so you do not have to repeat the context in each prompt.

Place the rules in a sheet named .rules, with one instruction per cell down column A. You can group longer lists under headings prefixed with ##. The create workbook rules option in the prompt box inserts a sheet with placeholders.

Because the rules are stored in the workbook, a colleague who receives the file receives them too. The sheet must currently remain visible: Copilot stops reading it if you hide it.

Advance your skills in Copilot in Excel by reading more of our detailed content.

Skills save instructions for processes you want to repeat across workbooks. Open Skills from the prompt box to see the built-in options, or call a skill by typing @ followed by its name. You can still call a disabled skill with an @mention.

Microsoft’s @brandkit applies an organization’s approved colors, fonts and logo if the company has set up a brand kit in Microsoft 365. @themedesign applies a coordinated palette to cells, tables and charts. The library also includes finance skills for three-statement models and comparable company analysis.

Under Formulas, you may see Python skills that let Copilot insert Python formulas and outputs into the workbook. Their availability is still rolling out, so the options shown can differ between users.

The review finds custom skills more useful than the skills library. A basic custom skill needs written instructions rather than code. For a monthly sales summary, Copilot can use those instructions to create a sheet with grouped revenue, each region’s percentage, a table and a related chart.

Copilot creates the required skills folder in OneDrive. You can write the skill file in Notepad or a similar editor. Its front matter contains the skill’s name and a description of when Copilot should use it. The body underneath contains the instructions.

Each skill needs its own subfolder, named to match the skill name in the front matter. Save the file as skill.md, then refresh Excel to find and turn on the skill. Custom skills are available in Excel for Windows, Mac and the web, although access can depend on your license, update channel and organizational settings.

Copilot can draw context from the web, your Microsoft 365 work account, Power BI and external connectors. Web search returns links to the pages it used. The Work source can search files, emails, meetings and conversations you already have permission to access. It is intended for eligible commercial Microsoft Copilot accounts.

Power BI has its own connection route, so Copilot can analyze report data without a manual export. In the add-content menu, all sources are allowed by default, but you can filter for Power BI and select a data set. Copilot can answer questions about it or insert editable tables, charts and other Excel elements.

Federated connectors retrieve external information in real time without first indexing it in Microsoft 365; examples include LSEG and Moody’s. Synced connectors instead index content from external business systems and are managed by an organization’s IT department. They should appear among the available sources if your organization has configured them and you have permission to use them.

Copilot in Excel requires an internet connection, a supported Microsoft 365 subscription and a current version of Excel. Power BI access follows existing permissions, including applicable row-level security. If Power BI is missing from the menu, an administrator needs to turn on Fabric data for Copilot in Excel. My Online Training Hub warns that a polished report is not necessarily accurate and recommends checking Copilot’s calculations rather than assuming it checked its own work.

If you want more control over how AI works with your spreadsheets, Copilot in Excel is worth a closer look for applying your working conventions and drawing on information beyond a workbook.

XREAL Aura glasses put digital screens in view while letting wearers see their surroundings through the lenses. They can display Android apps, computer desktops and games, with hand tracking for navigating windows. In his hands-on review, Steven Sullivan explores how the Aura performs across everyday productivity, media consumption and gaming, including its PC VR capabilities.

Explore how wireless virtual desktops can add computer displays and what the connection requires. As well as gaming options, including PC VR and compatible controllers, so you can see which experiences suit your setup. Finally, compare the Aura’s puck overheating and limited VR field of view with its display and gaming capabilities.

The XREAL Aura uses optical see-through lenses with a 70° field of view, 1200p per eye and up to a 120 Hz refresh rate. Prescription support ranges from -10 to +4 diopters. Cameras enable fixed-in-place windows and hand tracking, which worked much better in testing than it had in June. Gemini screen sharing can answer questions about an app or computer screen. The Aura can show five Android app windows at once. The $24.99 Virtual Desktop app supports up to three wireless Mac or Windows displays; testing found low latency and clear image quality. The Aura supports streaming services, Android games and wireless PC VR. Spatial view converts 2D content to 3D, and spatial audio places sound according to window positions. VR controllers are not yet supported, and some apps had glitches in testing. The Aura is rated for up to five hours of productivity or closer to three hours of intensive use. In testing, the puck showed an overheating warning after about 15 minutes of intensive VR or AR gaming in a pocket; the 70° view was also too narrow for full VR immersion.

The XREAL Aura uses optical see-through lenses, similar to the XREAL Air, so you see your real environment directly behind digital windows. In testing, the Aura’s lenses were light enough for indoor use with transparency turned all the way up. Flat X Prism optics also prevent reflections of your legs or feet on the ground beneath you.

The Aura glasses include three interchangeable nose-pad sizes, a prescription lens insert, a braided USB-C display cord and a lanyard for the puck. Cameras support six degrees of freedom and hand tracking, so you can walk around screens that stay fixed in place.

You pinch to select, swipe to scroll and look at your hand while pinching to open the main menu. In testing, hand tracking worked much better than it had in June. You can also remove app instances, arrange windows neatly and open Gemini or Circle to Search.

Circle to Search can identify real-world objects. With Gemini screen sharing, the assistant can see an app or computer screen and answer questions about it. For example, Gemini can see Google Docs and give you instructions for creating a table.

A wired PC or Mac connection to the XREAL Aura puck gives you one large computer display alongside four Android apps. For more computer displays, Virtual Desktop connects the glasses wirelessly to a computer. The app must be installed on both devices, and both must be on the same Wi-Fi network.

Virtual Desktop costs $24.99 on the Google Play Store and is free on the computer. The wireless connection also leaves the puck’s connection slot available for charging.

On the Aura, Virtual Desktop supports Mac and Windows and can show up to three different computer displays wirelessly. You can resize and position a display, orient one or more vertically, and use the computer’s keyboard and trackpad or mouse. A large vertical display can hold two horizontal windows stacked on top of each other.

In testing, the wireless desktop had low latency and clear image quality. Virtual environments include outdoor settings, a modern apartment at different times of day, and personal or commercial cinema rooms. A Bluetooth keyboard also works with the Aura itself; you can place the puck beside it and use the puck as a trackpad.

The Aura can show five Android app windows in the foreground at once, while more apps remain in the background tray. Opening a sixth foreground window closes one of the visible ones. Voice search worked in testing, and an Apple Magic Keyboard provided a faster way to type than hand tracking or selecting keys with a controller.

Here are additional guides from our expansive article library that you may find useful on XREAL Aura.

The Aura can play streaming services through Chrome, including Netflix, and has individual apps for Paramount Plus, HBO Max and Prime Video. YouTube’s theater mode places comments and related videos beside the main window. In testing, copyright restrictions blocked screen recording from the three named streaming apps, producing a black screen in the recording.

Spatial view converts app content from 2D to 3D. You can turn it on for an individual app using the cube-shaped control above its window or apply it broadly through quick settings. It also works with Android games.

The Aura has Bose sound and spatial audio, which places audio sources according to their window positions. In testing, a video and music could be heard as separate sources rather than blending together. Placing a music window above a game made the music appear to come from the game’s direction.

The Aura runs Android games including Minecraft, Knights of the Old Republic II and Star Wars Castles. For controller-compatible Android games, you can connect an Xbox or PlayStation controller over Bluetooth.

Chrome can open Xbox Game Pass for streaming, while Steam Link can stream games wirelessly from a PC. Xbox-streamed games run on Xbox servers; Steam Link games use the PC’s hardware. In testing with a gaming handheld wired to the puck, a heavily modded Fallout 4 kept running while a YouTube music window and a separate game-tips window were selected. No audio stutters were heard.

Virtual Desktop can also connect the Aura wirelessly to a PC for full VR games. The glasses do not yet support VR controllers, but Xbox and PlayStation controllers work. Subnautica ran with gamepad navigation while allowing you to look around at human scale; it launched better through Virtual Desktop on the Aura than it had on the Steam Frame.

Other experiences include the Cosmos app’s black-hole content and Galapagos VR. In Galapagos VR, you can change time to see how the islands formed, move tectonic plates in a 3D model and speak to a Charles Darwin AI. A piano overlay places notes over a real piano and uses the microphone to check what you play.

Some apps had problems in testing: a boxing game failed to register punches, a drumming game was inconsistent, and Spotify sometimes continued playback without sound until it was reopened. YouTube music did not have the same audio problem. The review does not consider the glitches an Aura issue, though the cause is unknown and app compatibility with Android XR is one possibility.

The Aura is rated for up to five hours of productivity with the puck, or closer to three hours for gaming, VR, media and other intensive use. You can charge it while using it, and the glasses did not come close to running out during testing.

The review’s biggest concern was overheating. During intensive VR or AR gaming, the puck showed a warning after about 15 minutes in a pocket, although it did not overheat all the time during intensive use. Keeping the puck outside a pocket during demanding tasks may help reduce the risk of overheating.

The included lanyard lets you wear the puck around your neck. Placing it on a table instead leaves a cable that you could trip over or pull out. A software update is a possible fix for the pocket overheating.

The 70° view was sufficient for flat-screen games and productivity windows, but too narrow for full immersion in VR games because the real surroundings remained visible. Comfortable light blockers could address that limitation. The XREAL Aura glasses were comfortable enough for extended wear in testing, but the puck’s overheating and limited VR field of view are important conditions to weigh against their productivity and gaming capabilities.

Apple’s MacBook Pro OLED XDR introduces a series of firsts to its iconic laptop lineup, including an advanced tandem OLED display and touchscreen navigation. These features mark a significant evolution for the MacBook Pro, alongside a lighter chassis design, extended battery life, and the integration of the powerful M5 Pro and Max chips. However, its premium price point and hardware limitations raise important questions about its overall value, particularly for legacy MacBook Pro users. In the video below, Andrew Ethan Zhang explores the key features, core strengths, and notable drawbacks of this high-end workstation.

Tandem OLED XDR Panel: Delivers up to 2,000 nits peak brightness and true absolute blacks, though low-frequency PWM dimming (240Hz) has sparked eye-strain concerns for sensitive users. Native Touch Integration: Brings Multi-Touch gestures directly to macOS for the first time, though app optimization remains limited. M5 Pro & Max Powerhouses: Supercharged by Apple’s latest silicon architecture, featuring advanced hardware ray tracing and dedicated Neural Accelerator cores. Shedding Weight: Engineered into a thinner, 15% lighter form factor that features a returning classic glowing Apple logo.

The PROLED XDR display is undeniably the centerpiece of the new MacBook Pro, utilizing a tandem OLED architecture that combines self-illuminating pixel layers to achieve unparalleled contrast and spec-busting brightness. It delivers true-to-life color reproduction, making it an extraordinary tool for professional colorists, photographers, and HDR video editors.

However, this transition introduces technical challenges. Glossy panel reflections can prove distracting under harsh lighting (though an optional nano-texture glass coating is available to mitigate glare). Furthermore, technical benchmarks and user reports have highlighted that the display uses a 240Hz Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) dimming cycle at lower brightness settings, which can trigger headaches, nausea, or eye fatigue for users sensitive to screen flicker.

For the first time on a Mac, Apple has integrated a touch-sensitive panel supporting direct Multi-Touch gestures for scrolling, pinching, and navigating. While this adds flexibility for casual browsing and interacting with UI elements, macOS remains fundamentally built around keyboard and trackpad inputs. Most professional desktop applications are not optimized for touch, and the deliberate omission of Apple Pencil support means digital artists cannot use the screen for precision drawing. Additionally, physical screen wobble during heavy tapping can occasionally detract from an otherwise premium workflow experience.

Apple has successfully re-engineered the MacBook Pro chassis, making it noticeably thinner and over half a pound lighter than its predecessor without sacrificing port selection or thermal efficiency. Slimmer bezels frame the display, while the webcam housing transitions to a functional Dynamic Island interface. In a nostalgic nod to classic Apple design, the iconic glowing Apple logo has returned to the rear lid, achieved via a custom internal light source engineered specifically around the backless requirements of the OLED panel.

Under the hood, the MacBook Pro OLED XDR is driven by the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, offering staggering single- and multi-threaded processing speeds. Equipped with enhanced GPU shader cores, a third-generation ray-tracing engine, and integrated Neural Accelerators, the machine shreds through 3D rendering, complex software compilation, and local AI model workloads effortlessly. Under sustained heavy loads, the updated thermal architecture manages heat efficiently, though active cooling fans will spin up audibly during maximum loads.

Despite the immense brightness capabilities of the tandem OLED panel, power efficiency remains a hallmark of Apple Silicon. The machine delivers up to 24 hours of total battery life depending on usage patterns, easily sailing through intensive mixed workflows on a single charge and freeing mobile professionals from constant wall tethering.

Starting at $2,899 / £2,899 for the 14-inch base configuration with an M5 Pro chip, the OLED XDR lineup commands a clear $400 premium over traditional Mini-LED models. When scaling up to fully maxed-out 16-inch M5 Max variations featuring massive memory pools and vast storage tiers, prices can climb steeply. For businesses and working professionals whose daily output relies directly on elite display accuracy and raw compute power, it serves as a powerful income-generating investment. However, casual users or owners of recent M-series MacBooks may find the generational leap harder to justify at this price bracket.

Despite its technical brilliance, prospective buyers should weigh a few critical factors:

This laptop is built explicitly for creative directors, mobile power users, and enterprise professionals who demand absolute peak screen fidelity, massive thermal throughput, and state-of-the-art port connectivity. Conversely, users sensitive to OLED flicker or those who do not require bleeding-edge graphics pipelines may prefer to stick with traditional display alternatives.

The MacBook Pro OLED XDR represents a monumental shift in Apple’s laptop strategy, marrying touchscreen capabilities with breathtaking tandem OLED visuals. While its high cost and niche display trade-offs require careful consideration, it firmly establishes a new benchmark for professional mobile workstations.

Google has described an internal cleanup system that finds outdated project notes that can send coding agents into unrequested work. The system is not publicly available, but Claude Code users can apply similar checks to their own project files. Stale instructions can lead an agent away from its assigned task, even when the requested work is eventually completed, according to AI Labs.

Explore how a source-of-truth rule helps Claude resolve conflicts between code and older plans, and how ticket status preserves room for unfinished work. The preview also covers a sweep skill that checks project notes against code and history, reports potential conflicts for review, and archives approved removals rather than deleting them outright.

Claude Code reads project instructions and plans into its context, so outdated notes can lead it to make unrequested changes. Google found that about one in seven sessions encountered a bug note; when agents pursued a note, more than four times out of five nobody had requested it. Side-quest sessions used 77% more tokens and took more than twice as long as sessions that stayed on task. A study found that Claude Code and Codex followed an outdated project file instead of the app nine times out of 10. Researchers also found that agent-written instruction files increased task costs by about 20% without improving performance. In testing, a rule to trust code over conflicting plans reversed the nine-out-of-10 result. Ticket statuses, instructions to leave unrelated work alone, and fresh sessions can also help keep work on track. Google’s cleanup agents checked bug records and code history before proposing note removals; engineers accepted more than 95% of suggestions. A proposed project sweep similarly checks plans and notes, reports potential issues for approval, and archives unneeded files.

Claude Code reads project files to plan a task before it starts building. It loads CLAUDE.md at the start of each session and can also read plans and requirements in the specs folder. Everything it reads enters its context, including instructions or notes that no longer match the app.

An old bug note or abandoned feature plan can give an agent work that nobody requested. Even a correct, unsolicited change can create work for you: the agent might alter something you meant to keep as it was, or implement a feature you planned to build differently.

Google calls these diversions side quests. To measure them, it examined developer notes in code that linked to bug records. It checked whether each bug had already been fixed and whether an engineer had asked the agent to address it.

Across millions of sessions from thousands of Google engineers, about one in seven sessions encountered one of those notes. Google found that when an agent pursued a note, nobody had asked it to do so more than four times out of five.

Of the side quests Google measured, 41% pursued already-fixed bugs and 57% pursued bugs that were still open without a request to fix them. Compared with sessions where the agent stayed on task, sessions with a side quest took 70% more actions, used 77% more tokens and took more than twice as long. An agent can still complete the requested task after a diversion, so you may not notice the extra work.

A study found that Claude Code and Codex followed an outdated project file instead of the app nine times out of 10. In the reviewed project, an agent likewise continued to follow CLAUDE.md when it disagreed with the app.

The size of the instruction file can matter too. Claude reads the whole file in each session, including sections unrelated to the task. Researchers found that agent-written files of this kind made each task cost about 20% more, without improving agent performance. As rules accumulate, they can also contradict each other, leaving Claude to choose between them without asking.

Claude’s memory adds another source of old information. It saves notes when corrected, and those notes do not expire. In a second brain made up of notes, there may be no app against which you can check whether an old entry is still accurate.

Even current project files do not prevent a session’s context from accumulating failed attempts and other old material. Chroma found all 18 models it tested became less reliable as context grew longer. People have also reported completed plans returning when a long Claude session is compacted.

Requirements can change faster than project documents. After a change in direction, an agent can build an email-only login while leaving a requirements document that still calls for Google sign-in. A later session reviewing the plan could mistake the dropped option for unfinished work.

Explore further guides and articles from our vast library that you may find relevant to your interests in Claude Code agent workflows.

The proposed setup puts a source-of-truth rule in CLAUDE.md: Claude should trust the existing code over a conflicting plan and report the difference. In testing, this rule reversed the earlier nine-out-of-10 result, with agents following the code instead of the outdated file.

Ticket status gives that rule an exception for unfinished work. Marking a ticket completed, in progress or not started helps Claude interpret a feature that appears in a plan but not in the code. If a ticket is in progress, Claude can follow its plan rather than treat half-built code as the finished design.

Another CLAUDE.md rule can tell Claude to leave unrelated work alone. In one test, Claude Code did no extra work when told what to leave untouched; without that line, it exceeded the request much more often.

For a request that is not already a ticket in the specs folder, a further rule can require Claude to compare it with existing plans before building. If the request overlaps with or contradicts a plan, Claude can flag the conflict and ask whether to proceed, giving you a chance to update the document.

AI Labs also recommends a fresh session for each task, including the move from planning to building. That keeps failed attempts from an earlier task out of the new session’s context, although it does not remove outdated notes already stored in the project.

Google built agents to search files for notes about bugs that had been fixed or dropped. A note that appears old can still be important, such as a warning that a bug may return if surrounding code is removed. Before suggesting deletion, Google’s agents checked the bug record and the history of changes to the relevant code, including changes from years earlier.

An engineer reviewed every proposed removal. Over six months, the check cleared thousands of notes, and engineers accepted more than 95% of the suggestions.

You can ask an agent to create a sweep skill that applies a similar history check to project plans and notes. The skill compares them with the current app and project history, then reports potential issues instead of immediately fixing them. If there is no proof that a note is outdated, the proposed skill leaves it alone.

Claude places the skill in the skills folder inside .claude, with its rules and phases in SKILL.md. Before reporting findings, the setup sends the claims to a checking agent without the main agent’s suspicions. It lists a memory or rule that conflicts with code separately for you to resolve, rather than automatically labelling it outdated.

After you approve the report, sweep moves unneeded files into an archive retained as a record. A hook runs a script before the agent reads, searches or edits, blocking reads of archived files. In the reviewed app, sweep found that CLAUDE.md still named a products page and its old locations after the page had been moved to the catalog.

Google’s system is not open for everyone to use, so reproducing the approach requires a setup in your project. You can use Claude Code’s monitor and loop features to ask Claude to build a similar system, but they stop when the session closes and cannot keep checking over days or weeks. The sweep skill and the other materials are available through the AI Labs Pro community.

If you use Claude Code and want help finding outdated project notes and plans, the sweep skill is worth a closer look.

The Xbox Ally X and Xbox Ally X20 are handheld gaming PCs built around the same Ryzen AI Z2 Extreme processor, but they differ in cooling design and display technology. In a four-game comparison, the X20 ran cooler and often delivered slightly steadier or higher performance than the original, according to GameTechPlanet.

Compare frame rates at 17 and 25 watts across the four games, then examine what the Cyberpunk result adds at 35 watts. The breakdown also considers how GPU clock speeds may affect performance and how the X20’s OLED display and revised controls differ from the original’s IPS screen and inputs.

Both handhelds use the Ryzen AI Z2 Extreme and have 1080p displays, but the X20 replaces the original Xbox Ally X’s IPS screen with OLED. OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra has just been launched and has drawn mixed assessments, with benchmark costs and coding results presenting different pictures of its performance. Below David Ondrej compares high and extra-high reasoning settings and their benchmark results to identify a starting point for coding or everyday requests. Learn more about how GPT-6.2 Astra handles creating interface designs and response-length problems to understand where task results may fall short.

Astra leads Agent’s Last Exam at about $2, compared with $60 for Fable, and leads Claude on Terminal Bench Science. On the Artificial Analysis Index, Fable scores 64.6 versus Astra’s 60.2 but costs seven times as much. Fable 5.2 leads Frontier Code, where Astra ranks around the middle. On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Astra is slightly better than GPT-6 Astra, while Soul is down three points. Dan Shipper reported that his team found the release disappointing compared with Fable 5.2: Astra frequently seemed to stop too early on coding tasks and appeared to make writing too brief. Other people reported positive experiences. OpenAI advertises Astra as capable of self-improvement, and its system card calls the model an early milestone toward fully automated self-improvement. Astra writes faster kernels for OpenAI’s own chip. David Ondrej’s Cloud Room is a free, open source AI coding environment supporting multiple agent harnesses. Using Astra at extra high, he created a daily Cloudflare security loop for its repository in two minutes and 46 seconds; he recommends testing Astra and Sol on individual workflows.

On Agent’s Last Exam, Astra leads the chart at a cost of about $2, compared with $60 for Fable. Astra also leads Claude on Terminal Bench Science, where Claude costs much more. Astra’s extra-high reasoning setting outperforms its max setting there, and max performs worse than extra high on some other benchmarks. Extra high may be a good default for Astra, particularly for coding, while high is recommended for most typical tasks.

On the Artificial Analysis Index, Fable scores 64.6 at max against Astra’s 60.2, but costs seven times as much. Fable is also slightly ahead on Bench CAT mechanical engineering at a much higher cost. On Automation Bench, Gemini 4 Carbon takes the top position.

Frontier Code tells a different story. Fable 5.2 leads, reaching its highest score at extra high, while Astra sits around the middle. Soul at max reaches a similar or possibly higher score than Astra on that chart. Sol also appears to offer strong agent-work performance for its price on LiveVal, where Astra appears to lead, although Fable and Gemini 4 Carbon are absent. Sol is expected to be a cost-efficient competitor to Opus, with extra high a potentially useful default.

The Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index presents a less flattering picture, although it is one coding benchmark rather than a measure of all capabilities. Astra is slightly better than GPT-6 Astra on the index, whose scores are rounded to whole numbers. Sol is down three points.

Those results prompted criticism of OpenAI’s progress, especially given the time taken to release the models. Opus 5.5 matches Fable on that coding index, even though Fable 5.2 is considered more intelligent and more performant overall.

Usage limits also shape that comparison. The creator says they use four subscriptions and had reached Fable’s limits on two of them. When comparing one $200-a-month Claude subscription with four subscriptions at that price, they favor Opus 5.5 for its coding, design, speed and efficiency.

Dan Shipper reported that his team found the release disappointing compared with Fable 5.2 after working with the models for weeks. His team found Fable similar to Astra 6 on most of its coding benchmarks, but said it frequently seemed to stop too early on real coding tasks, frustrating end-to-end builds. Shipper also reported a step back in writing: Astra appeared to favor brevity so strongly that answers could be hard to understand or too short. His team found good default design instincts but difficulty producing varied designs.

OpenAI advertises Astra as capable of self-improvement and has made it public. A system card calls it an early milestone on the way to fully automated self-improvement, and Astra writes faster kernels for OpenAI’s own chip.

OpenAI appears to be taking a different approach from Anthropic, at least in part. Anthropic blocks its models from machine-learning tasks to discourage distillation and training other models, while OpenAI has released a model it advertises for self-improvement. The Epoch Capability Index places Fable and Astra among frontier models showing faster progress.

OpenAI’s positioning also reflects enterprise competition. According to reports, Anthropic has surpassed OpenAI in revenue and company valuation, reversing the position from last year when Anthropic was catching up. GPT-6.2 also reached 100% on ARC-AGI and Noam Brown praised it, although the creator questions whether OpenAI remains at the frontier.

In a Cloud Room task, Astra proposed animations for the interface displayed while an agent works. Its suggestions included a floating cloud, a wave of dots, a turning cube, shifting shapes and an orbit. The creator found the set underwhelming, although the shape-shifting idea showed some creativity.

A separate interface redesign produced a mix of results: one was clean and minimal, another confusing, and one resembled Codex. That resemblance may reflect a bias in the model’s designs. Astra displayed the first image batch inline but failed to do so for a later batch; they also think they may have intended to request real GIF animations.

In another run, Astra worked for 30 minutes and returned a very short answer rather than listing seven items. That experience echoed Shipper’s criticism of overly concise responses. Separately, a model spent 30 minutes auditing a project and found issues in 26 files. Another model found, applied and committed a small bug fix in about four minutes and 15 seconds.

David Ondrej recommends Cloud Room for people serious about AI coding and advises testing Astra and Sol on their own workflows rather than relying on others’ opinions. He favors Opus 5.5 for coding, design, speed and efficiency when paying for one $200-a-month subscription rather than four. His tests do not establish which model is best for someone else’s job; his advice is to try the models on that work.

If you are searching for an easy way to create 3D models from real life components, you might be interested in using a 3D scanner. in this demonstration of the new Elegoo M1 Ultra Scanner. A custom cover for a sim racing wheel hub starts with a 3D scan of the exposed mount and ends with a printed part designed to protect its pins and mounting surface.

Learn how tracking markers and blue laser scanning capture the hub’s dovetails and pin area, then how the resulting mesh is trimmed and simplified for CAD.

The M1 Ultra has three scanning modes: infrared and two blue laser options, one marker-free and one using markers. For accurate measurements, a blue laser mode is probably preferable. The wheel hub was scanned in blue laser marker mode at 0.1 mm real-time resolution using seven parallel lines. Tracking markers are recommended where possible for better results and easier scanning. The scan took about 10 minutes in the confined rig. A system with an NVIDIA 3060 Ti reached 30 FPS, compared with 10 FPS on a non-NVIDIA system. The point cloud was trimmed and processed into a mesh, then reduced from 9 million to 900,000 triangles so the CAD program could handle it. The cover and snap-in catch were modelled in Fusion 360. The cover locks in place, but the locking tab still needs to be retained before the spring can be used.

The Elegoo M1 Ultra, the company’s first 3D scanner, offers three scanning modes: infrared and two blue laser options, one marker-free and one using markers. Infrared produces a texture-mapped scan and could be the easiest mode. It could be used to make a color figurine from a scan of a person. For truly accurate measurements, one of the blue laser modes is probably preferable.

The scanner includes tracking markers, which are recommended where possible for better results and an easier scan. Applying and removing the dots is tedious, especially when they are placed around the object as well as on it.

For the wheel mount, markers went on the bottom, the sides of the rings, each dovetail face and the sides of the pin mounting area. The aim was to cover as many positions and faces as reasonably practical, so the scanner could see at least a couple of markers.

In blue laser marker mode, the project used a standard field of view for detail and point cloud mode, the best-resolution option for that setup. Real-time resolution was set to 0.1 mm, the scanner’s best setting, and the laser mode to seven parallel lines.

Fewer laser lines collect more data, but the seven-line setting worked well enough for this scan. Marker mode can also map color. That was unnecessary here because the scan would not be printed directly, and a filament color could be chosen for the black-and-gray part.

The scan took about 10 minutes. The wheelbase was attached to a rig tucked into a corner, so scanning had to be done from inside the rig, with little room to move the scanner. Even so, the initial scan captured a detailed front view in under a minute. The whole job could have taken one or two minutes without the effort to capture every angle, particularly around the dovetails and pins.

Fortunately, the scanner stops collecting data when it loses track and resumes once tracking returns, a behavior that worked particularly well in marker mode. A 3060 Ti system reached 30 FPS, making scanning easier than the 10 FPS obtained on a non-NVIDIA system.

Enhance your knowledge on Elegoo 3D scanners and printers by exploring a selection of articles and guides on the subject.

After scanning, the point cloud was trimmed to keep the dovetails and spindle, along with the full snout of the hub. The extrusion, custom motor mounts and wheelbase front plate were deleted because the cap did not need them.

The scanner’s one-click processing converted the remaining scan into a mesh. Hole filling and smoothing cleaned it up, followed by simplification and export. If you only want to replicate and print a scanned object, you can proceed after processing. A part that must fit the object needs further CAD work.

The first mesh contained 9 million triangles, more detail than the project needed. After an initial export, it was reduced to 10% of its polygon count: 900,000 triangles in a 44 MB file that the CAD program could handle. That was still more than appeared necessary, and a reduction to 5% or lower might have worked.

If you are searching for a 3D scanner to help you create 3D printable products and designs faster, the new Elegoo M1 Ultra Scanner is definitely worth checking out in more detail.

The Ace Magic G3 A mini PC pairs a 24-core processor with room for a low-profile graphics card. Allowing users and ETA Prime to replace its NVIDIA RTX 2000 with an Intel Arc B50. The NVIDIA card led most benchmarks, while the Intel card ran several games at 1440p high settings.

This hands-on comparison by ETA Prime covers the single-screw GPU swap and the PCIe 4.0 connection, so you can see what fitting the card involves. It also compares AI and game results, including the Llama 3.1 and Red Dead Redemption 2 runs. Finally, it explains what the $359 bare-bones price excludes when planning your build.

The G3 A has a 24-core processor and is available with an NVIDIA RTX GPU or as a $359 bare-bones system without a GPU, RAM or storage. The GPU can be swapped using a single screw, clip system and riser card. The Arc B50 supports PCIe 5.0 x8, while the G3 A provides PCIe 4.0 x8; the expected cost is only a couple of frames here and there. The RTX 2000 led the B50 by about 12% overall in Geekbench AI and scored 9,033 versus 8,765 in Time Spy. The B50 won in Llama 3.1, reaching 45.2 tokens per second versus around 36.8 for the RTX 2000. At 1440p high, Forza Horizon 6 averaged around 78 FPS on the RTX 2000 and around 73 FPS on the B50. In Red Dead Redemption 2, the B50 averaged in the mid-70s without FSR, while the RTX 2000 averaged around 66 FPS with DLSS quality. ETA Prime says the B50 works well in the G3 A, particularly for someone who already has the card, RAM and an extra M.2 drive. His tests favor keeping the RTX 2000 if already owned; he expects the more expensive RTX 4000 configuration to outperform both, though he did not test it.

The G3 A is available with an RTX GPU or as a $359 bare-bones system without a GPU, RAM or storage. Its main specifications and configurations include:

The RTX 2000 and Arc B50 use different architectures but share the same workstation form factor. The GPU assembly can be removed using a single screw and a clip system, with the replacement connected through a riser card.

The machine is somewhat limited by its TDP given the CPU inside. Windows settings showed Resizable BAR and 4G decoding were already active, so the swap is expected to avoid problems associated with those settings. The B50 supports an X8 PCIe 5.0 slot, while the G3 A supplies an X8 PCIe 4.0 slot. The expected cost is only a couple of frames here and there, because the card’s 16 GB of VRAM reduces the need to swap data back and forth.

In Geekbench AI, the RTX 2000 led the Arc Pro B50 by about 12% overall and about 10% in half precision. Its largest lead came in quantized testing, where it delivered a 31% uplift over the Intel card.

The language-model results were split. GPT OSS 20 billion ran at around 70 tokens per second on the RTX 2000 and around 44 on the B50. In Llama 3.1, the B50 reached 45.2 tokens per second, compared with around 36.8 for the NVIDIA card.

Both cards generated the same image. Their image-generation performance is expected to be fairly even if each runs it a few times. In Time Spy, the RTX 2000 scored 9,033 overall and 8,395 for graphics; the B50 scored 8,765 and 8,036 respectively.

Under GPU load, both cards drew around 68 to 70 watts, depending on the workload. The NVIDIA card came ahead overall across the benchmarks, with Llama 3.1 providing the B50’s win.

At 1440p high, Forza Horizon 6 averaged around 78 FPS on the RTX 2000 and around 73 FPS on the B50, without DLSS or XeSS respectively. The game supports DLSS frame generation on the NVIDIA card, but not XeSS frame generation on the B50.

Red Dead Redemption 2 favored the B50 in the runs shown. At 1440p high, the B50 averaged in the mid-70s without FSR; the game does not support XeSS. The RTX 2000 averaged around 66 FPS with DLSS set to quality.

Spider-Man 2 was closer: the B50 averaged around 72 FPS at 1440p high with XeSS quality, while the RTX 2000 reached the low to mid-70s with DLSS quality. Mortal Kombat 1 also ran well on the B50 at 1440p high without scaling.

Doom: The Dark Ages used more than 10 GB of VRAM on the B50 at 1440p high with XeSS quality. XeSS balanced or medium settings could also be options for that game.

Crimson Desert ran at 1440p high with ray tracing off and XeSS multi frame gen set to X3. The game felt good to ETA Prime at that setting; X4 was also an option, while X2 was expected to bring it just over 60 FPS. For most of the games discussed, X3 worked well on the B50, whereas X4 often makes things feel less smooth on a card of this class.

ETA Prime says the B50 works well in the G3 A, particularly as a small system for someone who already has the card, RAM and an extra M.2 drive. The bare-bones machine costs $359, but that price excludes those components. For someone who already has the RTX 2000 configuration, his tests favor keeping the NVIDIA card. He expects the more expensive RTX 4000 configuration to outperform both.

BI: Pola Belanja Online Bergeser ke Transaksi Bernilai Kecil

Bloomberg Technoz, Jakarta - Bank Indonesia (BI) melihat adanya indikasi pergeseran pola belanja masyarakat ke transaksi dengan nilai yang lebih kecil.

Deputi Gubernur BI Filianingsih Hendarta mengatakan hal tersebut tercermin dari pertumbuhan volume transaksi perdagangan elektronik atau e-commerce yang lebih tinggi dibandingkan kenaikan nilai transaksinya pada Oktober 2026.

"Kalau kita lihat tiket size-nya [rata-rata nilai transaksi] itu sedikit menurun. Jadi tiket size-nya itu cenderung makin kecil," kata Filianingsih dalam RDG Bulanan BI, Rabu (18/11/2026).

"Artinya ada pergeseran ke belanja yang bernilai lebih rendah. Jadi yang belanja banyak, tapi mungkin belanjanya juga gak banyak-banyak [banget]," sambungnya.

Sebagai catatan, BI mencatat volume transaksi e-commerce tumbuh 17% secara tahunan (year-on-year/yoy) menjadi 552 juta transaksi pada Oktober 2026. Sementara itu, dari sisi nilai transaksi meningkat 11,97% yoy menjadi Rp50,4 triliun.

KEBIJAKAN MINERBA Prabowo Mau 70% Manfaat IUP Dikuasai Negara, IMA Respons

Ekskavator Komatsu Ltd. memuat truk di tambang batu bara terbuka PT Exploitasi Energi Indonesia di Palaran, Kalimantan Timur./Bloomberg-Dadang Tri

Bloomberg Technoz, Jakarta – Asosiasi Pertambangan Indonesia-Indonesia Mining Association (IMA) meminta pemerintah untuk menilai secara komprehensif segala bentuk manfaat dan kontribusi yang dihasilkan dari kegiatan pertambangan dalam negeri.

Permintaan tersebut disampaikan sebagai respons atas pernyataan Presiden Prabowo Subianto akhir pekan lalu, bahwa negara sudah semestinya menguasai 70% manfaat dari penerbitan izin usaha pertambangan (IUP).

Indonesia is calling for stronger sustainable peatland governance through data harmonisation, management based on Peatland Hydrological Units (PHUs), and regional cooperation to prevent peatland fires and transboundary haze across Southeast Asia and the Western Pacific.

Dr. Agus Justianto, Chair of the Interim Secretariat of the International Tropical Peatlands Center (ITPC), emphasised that peatland management must be grounded in accurate and reliable data to support policymaking, restoration planning, and stronger international cooperation.

Trending Menteri LH Tindak Tegas Tambang Nikel di Raja Ampat, Tegaskan Komitmen Lindungi Pusat Keanekaragaman Hayati Dunia

“Indonesia has 24.6 million hectares of Peatland Hydrological Units, based on peatland hydrological mapping. Having a common data reference is essential to ensure that management planning, restoration targets, and measurement, reporting, and verification systems are built on a consistent foundation,” Agus said.

Agus made the remarks during a dialogue titled “Building Coordination for Multi-stakeholder Collaboration on Sustainable Management in Indonesia, Malaysia and Papua New Guinea,” organised under the Western Pacific Sustainable Peatland Management (SAGU) Project at the ASEAN Pavilion during the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, on Tuesday (17 November).

Dr. Bambang Supriyanto, Vice-Chair of the ITPC Interim Secretariat, explained that differences in data on peatland ecosystem coverage and forest and land fires must be assessed in light of the methodologies, geographical scope, and reporting periods used.

“Responsibility for addressing peatland fires and transboundary haze cannot rest with a single country. Shared responsibility is needed through partnerships between governments and businesses, consistent law enforcement, and stronger regional coordination to ensure effective fire prevention,” Bambang said.

Bambang also highlighted the importance of accountability in investment and operational activities related to peatland management, including cross-border investments.

According to Bambang, public-private partnerships must be supported by transparency, oversight, and law enforcement to ensure that peatland management does not create environmental risks affecting neighbouring countries.

Meanwhile, Dr. Vong Sok, Head of the Environment Division and Assistant Director of the Sustainable Development Directorate at the ASEAN Secretariat, stressed the importance of strengthening regional cooperation on sustainable peatland management and transboundary haze, which affects the environment, public health, and economies across ASEAN member states.

He noted that peatland fires require a collective approach involving data harmonisation, stronger early warning systems, and coordinated policies and preventive measures among countries.

“Addressing transboundary haze requires shared commitment and responsibility among ASEAN member states through the exchange of accurate information, stronger cross-border cooperation, and coordinated peatland fire prevention measures to protect the region’s environment and communities,” Vong Sok said.

Swetha Peteru, Senior Scientist and Principal Investigator of the Western Pacific Sustainable Peatland Management (SAGU) Project, highlighted the importance of collaboration among Indonesia, Malaysia, and Papua New Guinea in advancing sustainable peatland management based on science, landscape approaches, and community participation.

She emphasised that knowledge exchange, capacity building, financing, and monitoring are essential to maintaining peatlands’ ecological functions while improving community well-being.

“Through the SAGU Project, we are promoting cross-border cooperation that integrates peatland conservation, restoration, and responsible use to support local economies and the achievement of regional climate targets,” Swetha said.

The forum also explored opportunities to strengthen policies, climate finance, knowledge exchange, and capacity building in measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV) systems, climate vulnerability assessments, and the implementation of Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs).

Cooperation between Indonesia and Malaysia, as ASEAN member states, and Papua New Guinea, as an ASEAN observer, was considered important in strengthening the region’s collective contribution to implementing the Paris Agreement.

Looking ahead, regional collaboration through the SAGU Project and ITPC is expected to accelerate the adoption of landscape-based peatland management, data harmonisation, fire prevention, and community economic development aligned with the ecological functions of peatlands.

For Indonesia, these efforts form a strategic part of supporting the FOLU Net Sink 2030 target, strengthening climate resilience, and ensuring that peatland ecosystem protection delivers lasting benefits for the environment, communities, and the regional economy.

Indonesia has reaffirmed its position as a driving force in global climate action through forestry diplomacy grounded in tangible results, social justice, and innovative sustainable financing.

At the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, through mid-November 2026, Indonesia’s Ministry of Forestry delivered a strategic message: global climate ambitions must go hand in hand with the well-being of forest-dependent communities and fair international financial support.
